newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Prods Outlook - Heat is hot, gasoline dormant.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Prods Outlook - Heat is hot, gasoline dormant.

text.p: Cash prices of heating oil heated up Monday and halted for the moment an oil futures sell-off, but traders said however U.S. oil markets were still waiting for the seasonal lift off of gasoline demand.
"I'm focusing on heating oil. The gasoline market is mostly asleep," said one cash trader, noting cash differentials on heating oil firmed sharply on Monday.

The firming of differentials in Houston markets was enough to first stoke New York Harbor distillate differentials then NYMEX heating oil itself, which settled Monday a sharp 1.23 cents higher at 61.76 cents a gallon.

Traders cited continuing maintenance activity for U.S. refiners as one of the main reasons behind the firm distillate outlook, with refiner buying seen coming from all over the country and even from South America.

Additionally, news Citgo Petroleum Corp had a coking unit fire at its Lake Charles, Louisiana refinery last Friday evening helped distillate markets firm up and stop the early selloff in NYMEX crude and refined product futures.
"Wet distillate barrels are legitimately tight in the gulf. Then when you get a hiccup like Citgo it aggravates the volatility," another cash trader said.
"Citgo was one of the biggest (gulf) distillate buyers today, so people wanted to jump in front of them," he said.
Leading the list of regions pulling distillate barrels away from the Gulf Coast was California, where a number of refinery outages in recent weeks has tightened those markets.

Traders said San Antonio, Texas-based Valero Energy Corp appeared to be the company quick enough to blend up a cargo of the low sulphur, low aromatic diesel fuel burned only in California, though that could not be definitively confirmed.
Low sulphur diesel in Houston firmed by 2.50 cents a gallon Monday, trading at 2.25 over March NYMEX futures.
The U.S. midcontinent has also sucked volumes away from the Gulf Coast, due mostly to seasonal refinery maintenance, traders said.
But gasoline markets were "laying on their side," a third trader said.
"Other than the strong U.S. Gulf distillate market, there's not much going on fundamentally," he said.
Players said gasoline prices are suffering following a round of strong output given gasoline's relative attrativeness to distillates.
"I think gasoline has yet to pay the piper. There's too much out there. Yields have not switched over to distillate. They're running it full steam," another trader added.
He said gasoline will have to go through a "reality phase" in the next few weeks, enduring negative fundamentals.
"Given the high values of gasoline for this time of year and the fact that refinery turnarounds are already priced in, it will go a lot lower before it goes higher," he said.
-- Oliver Ludwig New York Energy Desk +1 212 859 1633
